prize_parts.citation: for theoretical proposals that showed how trapped ions and ultracold atoms can be used for quantum computation and quantum simulation

statement.case_for: Cirac and Zoller wrote the blueprint that turned quantum information from an abstract idea into an engineering programme on real physical systems. The 1995 ion-trap gate proposal and the later joint work on cold-atom, Rydberg and ion-based simulation defined how gates, readout and many-body simulation are framed across platforms, including the superconducting-circuit community I work in. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: two theorists, jointly authored work, no serious dispute about who conceived it. The ideas have been confirmed experimentally by many independent groups over three decades, so this is neither premature nor speculative. Having listened to colleagues I still place it first, but I accept that the opening rankings show broader support for B013 and B061, and I treat my preference as a judgement on conceptual originality and attribution clarity rather than a count of votes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is scope and overlap. The candidate bundles ion-based gates with cold-atom simulation, so a citation has to be drawn narrowly enough to be one achievement. The 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems (Wineland, Haroche) already covers much of the experimental ground the proposals enabled. It is also a theory-only prize, and the experimental groups that built the first gates and simulators would be left unrecognised. A committee that values a discovery delivered by nature or an instrument that changed measurement could reasonably rank B013 or B061 higher, and B013 has stronger first-place and top-three support than my own first choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B034 third and calls the Cirac-Zoller pair a compact, natural configuration whose theory was validated by experiments that are partly already prized (2012), while placing the lattice-clock candidate B061 first as a clean, concrete advance in measurement.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll that the Cirac-Zoller attribution is clean and that the 2012 overlap is the central issue. I read the overlap differently. The 2012 prize honoured the experimental control of single ions and photons, not the theoretical proposals for using them as gates and simulators, so the two are distinct. I also respect his case for B061: Katori and Ye are a tidy pair and the maturity is good. My reservation is that the case against B061 is the same overlap argument turned the other way, since optical clocks sit right beside the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion work. If the committee accepts that kind of adjacency for clocks, it should not hold it against Cirac and Zoller.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B013 first, arguing that nature delivered a new regime in twisted bilayer graphene, that a theory-plus-experiment prize fits, and that independent reproduction across moire platforms makes it mature despite the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity.
responses.response: I largely accept his case on originality and reproduction, and B013 is my second choice. Where I differ is on attribution. His own opening concedes that the credited set omits others, and the three-person limit forces a choice that excludes Yuan Cao, who led the 2018 experiments, and leaves out theorists with earlier related contributions. A pairing of Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is defensible, but it is far less clean than the two-name Cirac-Zoller credit. The unsettled origin of the superconductivity also means the citation would have to rest on flat bands and correlated states, not the headline physics. I would support B013 if the committee settles who is credited, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B061 first and B034 third, noting that the Cirac-Zoller credit is clean but that overlap with the 2012 prize and with the neighbouring cold-atom simulation entry could make the scope hard to define, and that theory-only character may weigh against it.
responses.response: The scope point is fair, and I would answer it with a narrow citation: the theoretical proposals for quantum computation and simulation with trapped ions and ultracold atoms, with no claim over the experimental lattice-gas work in B050. On theory-only, I do not think the committee has to avoid it where the theory supplied the organising idea, as Bistritzer and MacDonald would in B013. I disagree that the clock ranking should come ahead, because the clock result rests on instrument performance whose attribution among lattice-clock groups at JILA, Tokyo, PTB and SYRTE is not fully captured by two names. That may well be manageable, but it is not obviously simpler than my candidate.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube candidate B009 first on the grounds that it opened a new observational window, with Halzen and Spiering credited, while acknowledging that the source associations are still statistically modest and that a large collaboration complicates the allocation.
responses.response: I take the astroparticle argument seriously, since a new observational window is the kind of discovery the prize has often honoured. My concern is the one he states himself. Only a diffuse flux and a few source associations are established, and the founding credit for neutrino telescopes is spread across DUMAND, Baikal and IceCube pioneers, so a Halzen-Spiering pair risks omitting people who were decisive. I am not an expert in this area, and I would defer to him on the instrumentation, but on attribution and maturity I find B009 less settled than B034.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can define B034 as one achievement without drifting into the experimental ion and cold-atom work that the 2012 prize and B050 already touch.
How heavily the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) should count against a theory prize in the same area, versus the overlap of B061 with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
For B013, whether Yuan Cao or other early theorists should displace a named laureate, which I cannot resolve from the supplied credit list.
I am relying on my own recollection of the history rather than independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: I have documented professional links to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and to my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum, and I direct WACQT, which works on superconducting circuits. These bear most directly on B018 (circuit QED), where I would recuse myself from the discussion, and I have not proposed that candidate. I also note that Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile with respect to B034, B013 or B061.
